150.0.0.en: Alleluia. Praise God in His sanctuary; praise Him in the firmament of His power.

150.0.1.en: 1- At the beginning, the psalm calls all the faithful to praise God in His sanctuary. The sanctuary is the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, which is a type of the Church of the New Testament and of the heavenly Jerusalem, where the throne of the great God is. Praising in the sanctuary means being present before God and enjoying the sight of Him; and so we find in the presence of God the angels and the saints, for God is holy in His children who live in holiness.

150.0.2.en: 2- The firmament means the heaven of the planets and the stars, in which appears the power of God the Creator, who governs their revolutions and movements. For despite their enormous size they move with precision so that none of them collides with another, and they do not harm the inhabitants of the earth, who are human beings beloved of God. The firmament is also a type of the Church, in which there are many stars, that is, great saints. And the Church in her spirituality rises above the material world. So let us praise God in His churches and in the holy faithful who pray in them; that is, let us see God in the lives of those who pray, and glorify God. This is the second matter for which the psalmist calls the faithful to praise God.

150.1.0.en: Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him according to His excellent greatness.

150.1.1.en: 1- The third matter is the call to the faithful to praise God for His powers, that is, His angels in their different ranks, whose principal work is praise. As we contemplate their life and their praise, we imitate them, and so we live in purity and in the love of God as angels on earth.

150.1.2.en: 2- The fourth matter for which we praise God is the abundance of His greatness. He is exceedingly great, and His greatness surpasses everything on earth. The greatness of God appears in His works and His various creatures, in which appear great creativity and divine wisdom, whose traces man is still searching out to this day, especially in the creation of man. But the greatest of God's works is His love, which appeared in His incarnation and His redemption of man.

150.1.3.en: If only you would contemplate, even a little each day, the Cross and the redemption, which is a love surpassing the mind; this will call you to thank God and praise Him.

150.2.0.en: Praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with the psaltery and harp.

150.2.1.en: The trumpet (Sur): the horn, made from a ram's horn or from silver, with a loud sound.

150.2.2.en: The psaltery (Rabab): a stringed instrument with ten or twelve strings.

150.2.3.en: The harp (Oud): a stringed instrument, known by this name even now, a wooden box over which five double strings are stretched.

150.2.4.en: 1- The first means by which we praise God is the use of the trumpet, which is a type of the power of the word of God. It calls man to awake from his heedlessness and to prepare to fight the devil and to triumph over him. In addition to attentiveness in prayers and praises, there should also be sensitivity to others and service to them. The angel will sound the trumpet on the Day of Judgment to announce the second coming of Christ and the proclamation of His justice in rewarding the righteous and condemning the wicked (1 Thess 4:16-17; 1 Cor 15:52).

150.2.5.en: 2- The second means of praising God is the use of the psaltery and the harp. The twelve strings used in the psaltery are a type of the Apostles, so we imitate their conduct in the love of God and His service. It may consist of ten strings, which are a type of the Ten Commandments, by keeping which we are encouraged to praise God. As for the harp with its five double strings, it is a type of man's praise with his five senses, inward and outward; that is, man praises God with all his senses.

150.3.0.en: Praise Him with the timbrel and dance; praise Him with stringed instruments and organs.

150.3.1.en: The timbrel (Duff): it resembles a drum or a tambourine. It is an animal skin stretched over a wooden frame, and cymbals or bells may be fitted into the frame; it is played by striking it with the hands. Stringed instruments: these are the string instruments, which are played with the fingers.

150.3.2.en: The organ (Mizmar): one of the wind instruments, made of a piece of reed, or of pieces fitted together, with holes; the sound is produced by blowing while placing the fingers on the holes.

150.3.3.en: 1- The third means by which we praise God is the timbrel and the dance. The timbrel, with its skin stretched over wood, is a type of the disciplining of the body so that the spirit may grow; that is, the seriousness and spiritual striving by which we draw near to God, so that our spirits are lifted up by praise. As for the dance, it is the movements of the body that are offered in devotional dance as an expression of the body's sharing in glorifying God. Thus the spirit and the body share in praising God. But the Hebrew word translated here as dance has no known meaning, and in the Coptic translation used in the Church it is translated as "rows" (the plural of a row), that is, groups sharing together in praise; and this word means the sharing of the whole Church in praising God.

150.3.4.en: 2- The fourth means of praising God is the accompaniment of the stringed instruments and the organ. The strings are a type of man's nerves; that is, man praises with his feelings, because the nerves represent sensation in man. As for the organ, which produces sound by blowing, it is a type of man's tongue. So praise is with the feelings and with the tongue, that is, with words, and man shares with all his abilities in praising God.

150.4.0.en: Praise Him upon the loud cymbals; praise Him upon the high sounding cymbals.

150.4.1.en: The cymbals of sounding: two circles of metal, each of which is placed on a finger, and they produce sounds by being struck together.

150.4.2.en: The cymbals of acclamation: two rings or round plates that produce sound by striking one against the other, which is what is now called the cymbals used in the Church.

150.4.3.en: 1- The fifth and last means by which we praise God is the cymbals, which regulate the voices of the group of those who praise so that they may be united in the praise offered to God. They are a type of the gathering of those who praise into one praise, that is, the unity among those who praise.

150.4.4.en: 2- St. John Chrysostom says, "God commanded the use of musical instruments in the Old Testament because of their spiritual weakness, to stir them to holy zeal and to praise God. But now (in the New Testament), when man has reached spiritual maturity, he uses all the members of his body as musical instruments expressing what is in his heart of love and thanksgiving to God." It is understood from this that the Church inclines to the use of man's throat and tongue in praise, and these voices can be regulated by the cymbals and the triangle, but she does not use the various musical instruments in her ritual prayers.

150.4.5.en: If only, when you praise God every day, you would praise Him with your whole being, that is, with your feelings, your mind and your tongue, so that you may rise above earthly things and begin to taste the sweetness of heavenly things.
